questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't recovering the signing address from the signature enough on its own?
options: It is enough; the lesson states no other checks are necessary
Because the siwe library does not support signature recovery
Because it's only one of three checks — the nonce and domain also have to be validated, or SIWE's safety guarantees don't actually hold
Because Ethereum signatures cannot be cryptographically recovered at all
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that signature recovery is necessary but not sufficient — it's only one of three distinct checks a correct verification performs.

questions.q: What three things does `SiweMessage.verify()` resolve to, per this lesson?
options: address, balance, and chainId only
A single boolean with no additional information
success (boolean), data (the parsed message on success), and error (populated on failure)
token, refreshToken, and expiresIn
questions.explain: The lesson shows the exact real shape verify() resolves to: success, data, and error.

questions.q: Why does the code in this lesson pass `nonce: req.session.nonce` into `verify()`?
options: Because nonce is a required field with no functional purpose beyond satisfying the API's type signature
Because it sets the session's expiration time directly
To generate a new private key for the session
To tie the verification back to the specific nonce the server itself issued for this login attempt, rather than trusting whatever nonce is in the message
questions.explain: The lesson explains this directly: without passing the server-issued nonce, verify() would only confirm the signature is valid, not that it's valid for this specific attempt.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens if a backend checks the signature and domain but never validates the nonce against a server-issued value?
options: The login would always fail with an authentication error
The signature itself would become cryptographically invalid
Nothing changes — the nonce has no security function per this lesson
A signature captured once (through a log, browser history, or compromised script) could be replayed to log in again indefinitely
questions.explain: The lesson walks through this exact scenario: skipping the nonce check turns a one-time signature into a permanently replayable credential.

questions.q: What does the domain check specifically protect against, per this lesson?
options: A user forgetting their wallet's private key
A phishing site getting a user to sign its own SIWE message and then replaying that signed message against the real site's backend
A subgraph mapping handler using non-deterministic logic
An RPC provider returning stale block data
questions.explain: The lesson explains that without the domain check, a cryptographically valid signature obtained via phishing could still be submitted successfully to a different backend.
